Title: Terminal-Universe: Turning Agent Trajectoriesinto Scalable Terminal Environments
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.04148.pdf
Published: 2026-09-03T00:00:00.000Z
Author: Jie Wu; Zhenru Zhang; Beichen Zhang; Xuwu Wang; Yuhui Su; Mouxiang Chen; Peng Wang; Zhihai Wang; Que Shen; Hao Zhou; An Yang; Fei Huang; Yujiu Yang; Dayiheng Liu
Highlights:
As terminal-based code agents become increasingly prevalent, the corresponding agent trajectories have accumulated at scale, while realistic, executable environments remain scarce. However, environments are what agent post-training actually requires: each one can be re-queried into many verifiable tasks and provides the execution feedback, whereas a trajectory is a single frozen demonstration. Rather than generating environ ments from scratch, we observe that the tool-execution history in the existing agent trajectories exposes the structure and contents of the environments in which they ran, making it possible to reconstruct those environments from the trajectories themselves. Thus, we introduce Terminal-Universe, a framework which turns each trajectory into a reusable environment and explores it for synthesizing new tasks and continued in teractions. Specifically, Terminal-Universe replays the file operations recorded in a trajectory to restore each file before the agent modified it, yielding a partial workspace; a completion agent then supplies the missing files and dependencies. On this recov ered workspace, we both reconstruct the original intent task and synthesize entirely new ones. Besides, we also scale the tasks for the corresponding environment along two complementary axes: breadth and depth, to reproduce a routine pattern of real engineering practice. For breadth, we mine directional dependency relations between related environments and synthesize cross-workspace queries spanning multiple code bases, as developers routinely do in real-world development. For depth, we extend the initial single-turn query into a multi-round session that captures iterative user feedback and requirement refinement via a user agent. Applied to publicly available terminal agent trajectories, Terminal-Universe produces 37.3k task-sufficient environments. Su pervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-27B on this corpus improves single-round performance on Terminal-Bench 2.1 by 11.9 points and multi-round performance on EvoCode-Bench v2 MT@4 by 13.8 points.

3.1 Environment Reconstruction From the file and command operations recorded in a trajectory τ, we recover an executable workspace E b that approximates the environment E in which τ was produced. This recovery is inherently lossy, since unaccessed files, implicit system dependencies, and external network resources leave no direct trace. We therefore reconstruct in three stages: deterministic replay recovers the file states τ exposes directly, agentic completion supplies the latent context it omits, and environment filtering keeps only workspaces sufficient for the recovered task q. Stage 1: deterministic replay. Replay processes the read, write, and edit operations in τ in chronological order to recover, for each accessed path, the earliest and latest file contents visible in the trajectory. The reconstructed initial workspace E b
...
3.2 Re-querying 
While reconstruction yields executable environments, re-querying dictates how effectively their latent 
capability space is exploited. We introduce four complementary re-querying mechanisms, denoted 
throughout the paper as Intent Recovery, Single-WS, Cross-WS, and Multi-Round. Intent Recovery 
reconstructs source tasks, while Single-WS synthesizes new tasks within individual workspaces. Cross 
WS provides breadth by connecting related workspaces, and Multi-Round provides depth by extending 
an initial query into an interactive session.

Figure 2: Framework of Terminal-Universe. A recorded trajectory is replayed and completed into an executable workspace, which is retained only when it is sufficient for its task (left). The recovered workspace supports Intent Recovery, Single-WS synthesis that explores a workspace to propose novel task candidates, Cross-WS synthesis via workspace profiling and relation mining, and Multi-Round continuation that extends an initial query into an iterative session.

Cross-workspace synthesis. To synthesize tasks spanning multiple codebases, we discover directional dependency relationships across recovered environments. An agent first profiles each workspace’s technical domain and implemented capabilities. We then retrieve candidate pairs via TF-IDF nearest neighbor search, and employ an LLM judge to identify directional dependency edges where a target workspace lacks a capability already implemented in a reference workspace. We allocate exactly one task per pair. Each cross-workspace task pairs a writable target workspace with a read-only reference workspace mounted at a separate path. The task generator confirms that the
...
Depth expansion. Extend solved terminal tasks through user-agent follow-ups. 
Multi-round user queries. Beginning with an initial terminal query, we preserve the workspace across 
coding rounds and introduce a user agent after the initial response. The continuation process employs 
two coordinated mechanisms to ensure coherent and realistic multi-turn trajectories: 
1. Evolving task specification. The user agent maintains an explicit requirement tracker logging active, satisfied, and updated requirements. Prior to each follow-up, it updates this tracker by adding, modifying, or replacing constraints, maintaining contextual coherence as the workspace evolves.
...
2. Round-level verification and feedback. At each extension round, the user agent commits the updated specification, prompting an automated verifier to author round-level acceptance tests before the coding agent acts. Upon receiving the agent’s response, the test runner evaluates both new criteria and active regression checks. The solver agent is strictly isolated from test scripts and tracebacks; the user agent interprets the structured test results and translates any failure into natural, user-observable complaints. Intermediate failures are retained within the conversation history, providing realistic supervision for error diagnosis and recovery.
...
In this work, we present Terminal-Universe, a trajectory-based environment and task synthesis framework that reframes recorded agent trajectories from fixed demonstrations into recoverable, reusable execution environments. Through a two-stage process of deterministic replay and agentic completion, Terminal Universe restores latent workspace state, synthesizes new tasks within each environment, and expands them across workspaces for breadth and across rounds for depth. Empirical evaluations show that re-solving recovered tasks outperforms SFT on the source trajectories, while verifier-selected Single WS, Cross-WS, and Multi-Round trajectories improve both single- and multi-round terminal-agent performance. Overall, our findings demonstrate that recorded trajectories can be effectively repurposed into interactive execution environments, offering a scalable paradigm for synthesizing grounded agent training data without constructing environments from scratch.

Terminal-Universe introduces a framework to bridge this gap by converting existing agent trajectories into reusable, executable environments. Rather than manually curating repositories or synthesizing environments from scratch, this approach recovers the latent workspace state from the trajectory's tool-execution history. By restoring these environments, the framework can then synthesize a wide variety of new, grounded tasks that span multiple codebases and multi-round interactive sessions.

 Figure 1: The Terminal-Universe framework consists of environment reconstruction (recovering workspaces from agent traces) and re-querying methods (generating new tasks through single-workspace, cross-workspace, and multi-round synthesis).

Each of these has limitations. Repository-based methods are often restricted to repair tasks and depend on available version histories. Perturbation methods can create many tasks but struggle with variety. Synthetic generation often lacks the realism and architectural complexity of real-world software projects. Terminal-Universe offers a fourth path: using the rich interaction data already present in agent trajectories to "bootstrap" realistic environments.
...
The core insight of Terminal-Universe is that a trajectory $τ\tau$τ contains implicit information about the environment $EE$ E in which it was generated. Every time an agent reads a file, lists a directory, or edits a script, it reveals a piece of the workspace. The goal of reconstruction is to produce an executable workspace $E^\hat{E}$ E^ that approximates the original environment.
...
To make the workspace $E^0\hat{E}_0$ E^ 0​ fully executable, it often needs missing context—such as dependency configurations, auxiliary scripts, or parent directories—that the original agent never touched. Terminal-Universe employs an LLM-based "completion agent" to fill these gaps. This agent is provided with the partial workspace and the inferred task $qq$ q. Its objective is to restore the environment's integrity (e.g., adding a `pyproject.toml` or missing imports) without actually solving the task itself. This results in a completed workspace $E^\hat{E}$ E^.
...
Not every trajectory contains enough information to be useful. An automated judge inspects the completed workspace $E^\hat{E}$ E^ to determine if it provides enough context for a human or a capable model to solve the intended task. Only "sufficient" environments are promoted to the task synthesis stage.
...
1. Intent Recovery: The original task that generated the trajectory is reconstructed. While the source trajectory might have been noisy or inefficient, the recovered intent allows a stronger "teacher" model to generate a cleaner, optimal solution in the reconstructed environment.
2. Single-Workspace (Single-WS) Synthesis: The framework analyzes the files and structure of $E^\hat{E}$ E^ to brainstorm new, grounded tasks that could be performed within that specific repository, such as adding a feature, refactoring a module, or improving documentation.
3. Breadth Expansion (Cross-WS): Real-world engineering often involves multiple repositories. This method identifies pairs of workspaces where one depends on or complements another.
4. Depth Expansion (Multi-Round): Single-turn tasks are expanded into multi-round dialogues, simulating an iterative development process with a user agent providing feedback and refined requirements.
...
Traditional agent benchmarks often focus on a single repository. Terminal-Universe introduces "Cross-WS" synthesis to teach agents how to handle inter-project dependencies. The system profiles different workspaces to identify their domains and capabilities. It then uses a retrieval mechanism to find a target workspace $WtargetW_{target}$ W t a r g e t​ and a reference workspace $WrefW_{ref}$ W r e f​ that have a meaningful relationship.
...
To improve an agent's ability to handle persistent tasks and cumulative requirements, Terminal-Universe implements a "Multi-Round" synthesis axis. A dedicated "user agent" interacts with a "solver agent" over several rounds.
...
The user agent maintains an internal requirement tracker to ensure consistency. After each attempt by the solver, an automated verifier runs tests. If the tests fail, the user agent provides natural language feedback (e.g., "The output format is still incorrect; it needs to be JSON, not YAML"). This creates a training signal for error diagnosis and recovery. The sessions can involve evolving specifications, where the user asks for feature extensions or revisions to previous work, resulting in long-horizon trajectories that are far more complex than standard single-turn examples.
...
A critical component of the Terminal-Universe pipeline is the use of an "Agentic Verifier." For every synthesized task, a specialized agent authors a test suite (typically using `pytest`) within the task's environment. A task-solution pair is only included in the final training set if it passes these automated tests. This ensures that the SFT data consists of verified, high-quality demonstrations.
...
Terminal-Universe demonstrates that the vast amount of agent interaction data currently being generated can be transformed from static logs into a scalable, high-fidelity training resource. By focusing on environment reconstruction rather than just data collection, the framework allows for the creation of grounded, verifiable, and complex training scenarios that were previously difficult to obtain at scale.
...
The ability to synthesize cross-workspace and multi-round tasks prepares agents for the realities of modern software development, where requirements are rarely static and solutions often span multiple repositories. This methodology provides a roadmap for continuously improving terminal agents as more interaction data becomes available, turning every agent session into a potential building block for future intelligence.

Qwen's Terminal-Universe paper argues that terminal-agent trajectories are more useful when you reconstruct the workspace behind them, then generate new verifiable tasks from that environment.

That is the useful idea in Terminal-Universe, a new Qwen paper that hit Hugging Face Papers today as the #1 paper of the day. The paper starts from a practical bottleneck: terminal-agent trajectories are piling up, but reusable executable environments are still scarce. A trajectory is one frozen demonstration. An environment can be queried again, tested again, extended into new tasks, and used to train agents on feedback rather than imitation alone.
...
The paper describes a framework for turning terminal-agent trajectories into reusable terminal environments. Instead of treating a run as a one-time example of "what the agent did," it tries to reconstruct the workspace state in which the run happened.
...
| Step | What it produces |
| --- | --- |
| Replay file operations | A partial workspace before the agent changed it |
| Fill missing files and dependencies | A task-sufficient executable environment |
| Reconstruct the original intent | A query matching the original trajectory |
| Synthesize new tasks | More prompts grounded in the same workspace |
| Extend sessions | Multi-round interactions with iterative feedback |
| Train on the resulting corpus | Better terminal-agent behavior on benchmark tasks |
...
The reported scale is 37.3k task-sufficient environments. The paper says supervised fine-tuning Qwen3.5-27B on the derived corpus improves single-round performance on Terminal-Bench 2.1 by 11.9 points and multi-round performance on EvoCode-Bench v2 MT@4 by 13.8 points.
...
Those are paper claims, not independent benchmark confirmations. But the direction is important even before the exact numbers are reproduced: the training unit moves from "copy this past run" to "recover this workspace, ask new questions of it, and check what happens."

Title: Terminal-Universe turns agent traces into training worlds — AICrier
URL: https://aicrier.com/post/6z691bi2u39p4hvyfcjg
Published: 2026-09-06T00:00:00.000Z
Author: N/A
Highlights:
Terminal-Universe reconstructs executable workspaces from terminal-agent trajectories, then expands them into verifiable single- and multi-round training tasks. Its 37.3K-environment corpus improved Qwen3.5-27B by 11.9 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 13.8 points on EvoCode-Bench v2 MT@4.
...
Terminal-Universe makes a compelling case that executable environments—not just more trajectories—are the missing ingredient in coding-agent post-training.
...
- – Replays file operations to recover workspaces, then uses agentic completion to restore missing files and dependencies.
- – Converts one frozen trajectory into many tasks through intent recovery, cross-workspace queries, and simulated multi-round feedback.
- – Reported gains suggest environment diversity can matter more than simply expanding imitation data.
- – The approach could create a self-reinforcing data flywheel as stronger agents generate richer, more reusable workspaces.
- – The results remain primarily a research demonstration, with teacher-generated tasks and verification creating potential coverage and evaluation blind spots.
